q: Wednesday evening club race, ILCA 7s. On the first beat you are on port tack and misjudge a cross: Grey, close-hauled on starboard, has to bear away hard to miss your transom. No contact. You know you broke rule 10. What penalty do you take?
a: A Two-Turns Penalty, as soon as possible after getting well clear of the other boats
o: A One-Turn Penalty — that is the penalty for forcing a boat to change course without contact
No penalty — without contact there is no breach to pay for
Retire — a breach of rule 10 cannot be repaired by turns on the water
why: Rule 44.1: a boat that may have broken a rule of Part 2 may take a Two-Turns Penalty; rule 44.2 says when and how.

fig.note: Grey bears away to miss your transom

q: National championship, 470 class, second lap. Rounding the leeward mark cleanly, with no other boat within five lengths, your boom brushes the buoy. What is the penalty?
a: A One-Turn Penalty — one tack and one gybe, taken as soon as possible after getting well clear of other boats
o: A Two-Turns Penalty — two tacks and two gybes, the standard penalty on the water
A 20 % Scoring Penalty, shown by displaying a yellow flag until you finish
No penalty — touching a mark with the rig rather than the hull is allowed
why: Rule 31 forbids touching the mark; rule 44.1 gives a One-Turn Penalty for a breach of rule 31 alone.

fig.note: The boom brushes the mark; nobody else near

q: Leeward mark of a Melges 24 regatta in Split. You are the windward boat, overlapped with Red inside you. As you squeeze in, your boom hits Red's shroud and in the same moment your bow touches the mark. What penalty covers this?
a: One Two-Turns Penalty — when a boat breaks a Part 2 rule and rule 31 in the same incident she need not take the penalty for rule 31
o: Three turns — two for the contact with Red and one more for the mark
One turn only — touching a mark is the more specific breach and replaces the two turns
Retire — a boat that breaks two rules in one incident cannot take turns
why: Rule 44.1(a): a breach of Part 2 and rule 31 in the same incident is settled by the Two-Turns Penalty alone.

fig.note: Your boom hits Red, your bow hits the mark

q: J/70, Lake Garda. After fouling a boat on the run you take your penalty: you luff, tack, bear away, gybe and come back to course — then you do the second turn the other way round, starting with a gybe to the opposite side. Your tactician says the penalty is complete. Is it?
a: No — both turns must be made in the same direction; the second turn does not count
o: Yes — each turn had a tack and a gybe, and the rule does not care about the direction
Yes — as long as both turns are finished within two minutes of the incident
No — a penalty turn must always begin with a tack, never with a gybe
why: Rule 44.2: the required number of turns in the same direction, each including one tack and one gybe.

fig.title: Your penalty on the run
lines: Turn 1: luff, tack, bear away, gybe
Turn 2: gybe the other way, then tack

q: 29er, windward mark, 18 knots. You hit Blue while tacking in front of her — clearly your fault. You round the mark and the offset, hoist the kite, and only 150 m down the run, where it is quieter, do you take two turns. Blue protests. What will the protest committee most likely decide?
a: You are disqualified — the turns were not taken as soon as possible after getting well clear, so they do not count
o: No further penalty — you completed two full turns before finishing, which is all rule 44 asks
No further penalty — the rule says to get well clear first, and you did
A 20 % Scoring Penalty is added for the delay, but the turns otherwise stand
why: Rule 44.2: get well clear of other boats as soon after the incident as possible, then take the turns promptly; a delayed penalty is no penalty.

fig.title: Windward mark, Lake Garda
lines: Rounded mark and offset, hoisted kite
Two turns taken 150 m down the run

q: Melges 24 worlds, thirty seconds after the start, the fleet is tight. You are on port and foul a starboard-tack boat. You start spinning on the spot, in the middle of the pack, and three boats have to alter course to avoid you. What is wrong with that?
a: You should first have sailed clear of the other boats, and while turning you must keep clear of them — rule 21.2
o: Nothing — a penalty must start immediately after the incident, and the others must keep clear of you
Nothing — a boat taking a penalty has right of way over boats that are not
You should have waited until after the first mark; penalties are not allowed on the first leg
why: Rule 44.2: get well clear first; rule 21.2: a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of one that is not.

fig.note: You begin your turns inside the pack

q: Dragon, Saronic Gulf. Ten metres short of the finishing line you fail to keep clear of Red to leeward (rule 11). You cross the line, take two turns on the far side of it and sail off to the harbour. Have you finished?
a: No — after the turns your hull must come completely back to the course side of the line, and then you must cross it again
o: Yes — you finished when your bow crossed, and the turns after it complete the penalty
No — turns are not permitted near the finishing line at all; your only option was to retire
Yes — provided the turns were completed within the finishing area
why: Rule 44.2: taking a penalty at or near the finishing line, her hull must be completely on the course side before she finishes; definition Finish.

fig.note: Your turns are on the far side of the line

q: Palma, 20 knots, a 36-ft cruiser-racer. On port you hit a starboard-tack boat; one of her crew is taken ashore with a broken wrist. You immediately take two turns and carry on. Is that the right penalty?
a: No — because the incident caused injury, your penalty is to retire from the race
o: Yes — two turns is the penalty for any breach of a Part 2 rule, whatever the consequences
Yes, provided you also display a yellow flag and tell the race committee at the finish
No — with injury you must take three turns instead of two
why: Rule 44.1(b): if the boat caused injury or serious damage, her penalty shall be to retire.

fig.title: Bay of Palma, 20 knots
lines: You on port, hit a starboard boat
You took two turns at once

q: Club regatta on the river, 30-footers. Misjudging a duck, you T-bone Grey amidships: a 30 cm hole in her topsides, she retires and motors home. You take a Two-Turns Penalty and finish third. What should you have done?
a: Retired — you caused serious damage, so turns are not the applicable penalty and the protest committee will disqualify you
o: Nothing more — two turns were taken promptly and that settles a Part 2 breach
Taken one extra turn for the damage, three in all
Displayed a yellow flag and accepted a 20 % Scoring Penalty
why: Rule 44.1(b): serious damage means the penalty is to retire; a boat that takes turns instead is still liable to be disqualified.

q: Star class, crowded windward mark, 40 boats. You come in on port, foul two starboard-tack boats in the queue, but by forcing your way through you avoid the pile-up and gain about fifteen places. You take two turns and lose four of them. Is the penalty enough?
a: No — despite the turns you gained a significant advantage from your breach, so your penalty is to retire
o: Yes — two turns taken promptly settle any number of Part 2 breaches in one incident
No — you fouled two boats, so you owe four turns
Yes — but you must also show a yellow flag so the committee can add 20 %
why: Rule 44.1(b): a boat that gained a significant advantage in the race or series despite taking a penalty shall retire.

fig.title: Windward mark, Star fleet
lines: You on port, foul two starboard boats
You slip past the pile-up: +15 places

q: Optimist regatta, light air. Your bow nudges the transom of Blue, who is clear ahead of you on the same tack — a touch at walking pace, no mark, no damage. Blue says nothing and sails on. What does the basic principle of sportsmanship expect of you?
a: To take a Two-Turns Penalty anyway — a boat that breaks a rule and is not exonerated promptly takes the appropriate penalty
o: Nothing — a penalty is only required when the other boat hails "Protest"
Nothing — contact that leaves no damage is not a breach of any rule
To take a One-Turn Penalty — contact without damage counts like touching a mark
why: Basic principle Sportsmanship and the Rules, rule 12 and rule 44.1: you broke rule 12, so you take the penalty whether or not anyone protests.

q: Beat in a J/24 fleet. Red, on port, cannot cross you on starboard. You could have borne away behind her in good time but hold on and hail; the boats collide and Red's gunwale cracks. Red takes two turns. What about you?
a: You too may have broken a rule — rule 14, and with damage you are not exonerated — so you should take a Two-Turns Penalty as well
o: Nothing — the right-of-way boat is never penalised in a port–starboard incident
Nothing — Red has already taken the penalty for the incident, and one penalty per incident is enough
You must retire — any right-of-way boat involved in a collision with damage must retire
why: Rule 14: a right-of-way boat must avoid contact once it is clear the other is not keeping clear; rule 43.1(c) exonerates her only if there is no damage.

You could have borne away in time

q: The sailing instructions of a J/24 championship say that rule 44.3, the Scoring Penalty, applies. Rounding the leeward mark you fail to keep clear of a leeward boat. How do you take your penalty?
a: Display a yellow flag at the first reasonable opportunity, keep it up until you finish, and draw the race committee's attention to it at the finishing line
o: Take two turns anyway — the sailing instructions cannot replace the Two-Turns Penalty
Hail "Twenty per cent" to the other boat and continue racing
Display a red flag until you finish and report to the race office
why: Rule 44.3(a) and (b): the Scoring Penalty is taken by displaying a yellow flag promptly, keeping it until finishing and informing the race committee.

lines: Leeward mark, you are windward boat
You fail to keep clear — your breach
No damage, no other boat affected

q: Forty-nine boats are entered in a Laser regatta where the Scoring Penalty applies. You take it for an incident on the run and finish 7th. What is your score for the race?
a: 17 points — 7 plus 20 % of the DNF score (50 points), i.e. 10 points; the other boats' scores do not change
o: 8.4 points — 7 plus 20 % of your own finishing score
57 points — 7 plus 20 % of 49 entries is 9.8, rounded up to 50 added points
17 points — and every boat that finished behind you moves up one place
why: Rule 44.3(c): 20 % of the score for DNF (entries + 1), added to the boat's own score; the scores of other boats are not changed.

fig.title: Scoring Penalty taken
lines: SI do not specify another figure

q: A twelve-boat Dragon fleet. You take a 20 % Scoring Penalty and then finish last, 12th. The committee enters 15 points against your name. Is that right?
a: No — a Scoring Penalty may not make your score worse than the score for DNF, which here is 13 points
o: Yes — 12 points plus the penalty, rounded, is 15
No — the penalty is 20 % of 12, so you get 14.4 points
No — a boat that finishes last is not penalised further; 12 points stand
why: Rule 44.3(c): the penalty shall not be worse than the score for Did Not Finish.

q: Scoring Penalty allowed by the sailing instructions. At the gybe mark you lose control in a gust and hit the boat ahead; her bowman is cut on the forearm and needs stitches. Your crew hoists the yellow flag. Does that settle it?
a: No — when the boat caused injury or serious damage the penalty is to retire; the Scoring Penalty is not available
o: Yes — where the sailing instructions allow it, the yellow flag replaces every other penalty
Yes — but you must also do two turns because there was contact
No — for injury the penalty is 40 %, so you need two yellow flags
why: Rule 44.1(b) overrides rule 44.3: injury or serious damage means retirement, not turns and not a Scoring Penalty.

lines: You hit the boat ahead in a broach
Her bowman: a cut that needs stitches

q: You show the yellow flag at once after an incident on the first beat, but on the last run it blows out of the shroud and you do not replace it; at the finish you say nothing to the committee boat. The other boat protests. What is your position?
a: Weak — the Scoring Penalty requires the yellow flag to be displayed until you finish and the committee to be told at the finishing line; you have taken no valid penalty
o: Strong — you displayed the flag at the first reasonable opportunity, which is what matters
Strong — the committee boat should have seen the flag earlier in the race
Neutral — the protest committee will simply apply the 20 % for you
why: Rule 44.3(b): display the yellow flag until finishing and call the race committee's attention to it at the finishing line.

lines: Yellow flag up at once after the foul
Flag lost on the last run
Not replaced; nothing said at the finish

q: The notice of race of a big-fleet Optimist regatta says: "Rule 44.1 is changed: the Scoring Penalty, rule 44.3, replaces the Two-Turns Penalty." You foul a boat at the windward mark and, out of habit, take two turns instead of showing the yellow flag. The boat protests. Outcome?
a: You are disqualified — the specified Scoring Penalty replaces the turns, so your turns were not an applicable penalty
o: No further penalty — two turns is always at least as severe as a yellow flag
No further penalty — the protest committee just converts your turns into 20 %
A warning only, because you did take a penalty of some kind
why: Rule 44.1: the NoR or SI may specify the Scoring Penalty, in which case it replaces the One-Turn and Two-Turns Penalties.

You take two turns, no yellow flag

q: National championship, flag Z displayed with the preparatory signal. In the last minute before the start part of your hull is inside the triangle formed by the ends of the line and the first mark. The start is otherwise clean and the committee identifies you. What happens?
a: You get a 20 % Scoring Penalty without a hearing — and it stays even if the race is restarted or resailed
o: You are disqualified without a hearing
You must sail back round an end of the line before starting
You must take a Two-Turns Penalty as soon as you are clear
why: Rule 30.2: the Z flag rule — a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute gets a 20 % Scoring Penalty without a hearing.

lines: 0:40 to the start: your bow in the triangle

q: Flag U is the preparatory signal. At 0:30 you are inside the triangle and the committee notes your number; then too many boats are over and First Substitute goes up with two sounds. What happens to your penalty?
a: It is lifted — under flag U the disqualification does not apply if the race is restarted or resailed; you may start again
o: It stands — you are UFD and must not start the restarted race
It becomes a 20 % Scoring Penalty because the race is restarted
You may start, but only after sailing round an end of the line
why: Rule 30.3: disqualified without a hearing — except when the race is restarted or resailed.

q: Black flag preparatory signal. You are over in the last minute; the committee signals a general recall and then displays your sail number on the committee boat. What are your options?
a: None — you are disqualified (BFD) and may not sail the restarted race; if you do, the disqualification becomes non-excludable
o: Start again — a general recall wipes out all starting penalties
Start again, but do a Two-Turns Penalty right after the starting signal
Start again, accepting a 20 % Scoring Penalty
why: Rule 30.4: the black-flag disqualification stands after a general recall; a boat whose number is displayed shall not sail again in that race.

fig.title: Black flag start
lines: You in the triangle in the last minute
Your sail number displayed on the RC boat

q: Black flag race. At 0:45 your bow is well inside the triangle. At 0:20 the race committee hoists AP with two sounds and postpones the start. Does the black-flag penalty apply to you?
a: No — the penalty does not apply when the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
o: Yes — you were identified in the last minute, so you are BFD for this race
Yes, but it is reduced to a 20 % Scoring Penalty
No, but you must sail round an end of the line before the new start
why: Rule 30.4: the penalty does not apply if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

q: Flag I is displayed with the preparatory signal. With 40 seconds to go, you drift over the line near the pin. Your crew says: "Do a quick turn and go." What actually fixes the error?
a: Sailing to the pre-start side round an end of the line before you start — a penalty turn does nothing for a starting error
o: A One-Turn Penalty taken immediately on the course side of the line
A Two-Turns Penalty taken after the starting signal
Dipping back across the line anywhere, as under flag P
why: Rule 30.1: a boat on the course side in the last minute shall sail round an end of the line to the pre-start side before starting.

q: P flag start in a 36-ft cruiser-racer fleet. You did not notice flag X and sailed on; after finishing you learn you were on the course side at the gun. The owner suggests doing two turns before the committee boat "to be safe". Will that help?
a: No — a starting error is corrected only by returning and starting correctly; now you are scored OCS without a hearing, and no turns change that
o: Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty taken before the finishing line is removed closes any breach of the race
Yes, if the turns are completed on the course side of the finishing line
No — but you can take a 20 % Scoring Penalty instead of OCS
why: Rule 29.1 and definition Start: a boat that does not return and start correctly has not started; she is scored OCS under Appendix A.

a: A 30 % Post-Race Penalty — a written statement to the arbitrator or a protest committee member before the hearing begins
o: Take a 20 % Scoring Penalty by hoisting a yellow flag at the dock
Do two turns in the harbour in front of the committee boat
Nothing — once a protest is lodged only the hearing can penalise you
why: Appendix T1: a boat that may have broken a Part 2 rule or rule 31 may take a 30 % Post-Race Penalty any time after the race and before the hearing starts.

q: Beat in a Hobie 16 fleet off Bodrum. You are close-hauled on starboard; a port-tack boat ducks you late, her bow a metre from your stern, and her skipper hails "Protest!" You held a straight course throughout. What do you do?
a: Keep racing — if you broke no rule there is nothing to pay for; a hail of "Protest" only announces a hearing, which will decide
o: Take a Two-Turns Penalty — a boat that is protested must take a penalty or be disqualified
Retire — the starboard boat is responsible for any near miss on a beat
Hail "Protest" back at once, which cancels her protest
why: Rule 44.1 lets a boat that may have broken a rule take a penalty; a boat that broke none need not — the protest committee decides the facts.

q: Reaching leg, 470s. Red to leeward hails "Protest" and says you, the windward boat, touched her. You felt nothing but cannot be sure — the boats were very close. What is the sensible course of action under the rules?
a: You may take a Two-Turns Penalty now: a boat that may have broken a rule can take it, and if the committee later finds you did, you will not be penalised further
o: Wait for the hearing — once "Protest" has been hailed, turns can no longer be taken
Do not take turns — doing them is an admission and you would be disqualified anyway
Take one turn as a compromise, since the contact is uncertain
why: Rule 44.1 applies to a boat that 'may have broken' a rule; rule 60.5(c): a boat that has taken the applicable penalty is not penalised further.

q: You took two turns promptly after a windward–leeward incident with Blue, yet Blue lodged a protest anyway. The protest committee finds that you broke rule 11, that there was no damage and that you gained no advantage. What is its decision on your penalty?
a: No further penalty — you had already taken the applicable penalty for the breach
o: Disqualification — a protest that is upheld always ends in DSQ
A 20 % Scoring Penalty on top of the turns
A non-excludable disqualification, because you were protested after taking turns
why: Rule 60.5(c): a boat that has taken the applicable penalty shall not be penalised further, unless the penalty for the rule broken is a non-excludable DSQ.

q: After a collision at the leeward mark you took two turns at once. In the hearing the protest committee finds you broke rule 18.2 and that the other boat's pulpit was bent and her forestay fitting cracked — serious damage. What does the committee decide about your penalty?
a: Disqualification — with serious damage the applicable penalty was to retire, so your turns do not protect you
o: No further penalty — you took a Two-Turns Penalty promptly after the incident
A 20 % Scoring Penalty to reflect the damage
Retirement entered retroactively — RET instead of DSQ
why: Rule 44.1(b): serious damage means retirement; rule 60.5(c) protects only a boat that took the applicable penalty.

You took two turns on the water

q: A protest committee at a club championship finds that you broke rule 10 on the second beat and took no penalty at all. No damage, no injury, no advantage worth mentioning. What is the penalty it imposes?
a: Disqualification from the race — the default when a boat broke a rule and no other penalty applies; excludable in the series
o: A 20 % Scoring Penalty — the committee applies rule 44.3 for you
A Two-Turns Penalty to be sailed before the next race
A non-excludable disqualification, because you did not take turns
why: Rule 60.5(c): the protest committee shall disqualify a boat that broke a rule unless she is exonerated or another penalty applies.

q: Last race of a club series. At the final mark you deliberately sail into your rival so that your clubmate gets past her, then take a Two-Turns Penalty "to pay for it". Your rival protests under rule 2. Do the turns settle the matter?

o: Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty settles any breach of a Part 2 rule, whatever the intention
Yes, provided there was no damage and no injury
No — the penalty for a deliberate foul is four turns instead of two

A Two-Turns Penalty, which you may still take after the race
A 20 % Scoring Penalty without a hearing

q: Leeward mark, 470s. Blue is overlapped to windward of you and does not keep clear: she leans on you and pushes you onto the mark, which you touch with your hull. Who takes what?

o: You take a One-Turn Penalty for the mark and Blue takes two turns

Both you and Grey, two turns each
Nobody — Red had to bear away only slightly, so there was no breach

Yes — you take one turn as the boat that caused less of the contact
No — a right-of-way boat can never break rule 14

Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, since there was contact with a boat and with the mark

A turn must include two tacks and one gybe
A turn must start with a gybe when taken on a beat

Yellow — she was clear astern of you when the turns began
Neither — the normal Part 2 rules are suspended around a boat taking a penalty

No — after the starting signal rule 23.2 never applies
Yes — you broke rule 21.2 by not keeping clear of Blue

o: Retire from the race immediately

o: As RET — you retired as required, and the score can be discarded
As an ordinary DSQ that can be used as your discard
As DNF plus a 20 % Scoring Penalty

o: To take a Two-Turns Penalty, as for any breach of a rule while racing — rule 44 covers them all
To take a One-Turn Penalty, since rule 42 is in Part 4

q: You retire after causing serious damage at the gybe mark, in a 24-boat Dragon fleet. How is the race scored for you?
a: RET — points for the finishing place one more than the boats entered, i.e. 25; excludable as a discard
o: DNE — a disqualification that cannot be excluded from the series
DNF — the same as not finishing, with a 20 % penalty added
The points of the last boat that finished, plus one

q: On the final beat you cross a starboard boat by a whisker — you know you should have ducked — but she does not hail and nobody protests. You keep your 2nd place and tell the story in the bar. How do the rules see this?

q: Running in a 470 fleet, both on port. You are to leeward and luff sharply without giving Red, overlapped to windward, room to keep clear; Red reacts late and her boom hits your shroud. No damage. Who takes a penalty?

Only you — the boat that altered course is always the one at fault

The bowman — on a run the penalty is two gybes rather than a tack and a gybe

To take two turns before clearing the finishing line, since the report is incomplete
To lodge a written protest against the other boat

Yes — the rule only requires the flag to be displayed for at least one leg
No — the yellow flag must be hoisted before the incident is over

Yes — but it is halved to 10 % because the start was postponed
No — but you must sail round an end of the line before the new start

o: Yes — a U-flag disqualification stays with the race number, whatever happens later
Yes — only a general recall before the start removes it
No — but it becomes a 20 % Scoring Penalty in the resail

o: Yes — a rule 10 breach is carried over into the resail and can be heard there
Yes — you must take two turns at the start of the resail
No — but you are scored with a 20 % penalty in the resail

Signalling that she is retiring from the race
Acknowledging a rule 42 penalty signalled by the jury

None — only the boat that touched the mark owes a penalty

Nothing — contact with a sheet rather than the hull is not touching the mark
Take a Two-Turns Penalty — late mark penalties are doubled
why: Rule 31 covers any part of the boat; rule 44.2 requires the penalty as soon as possible after the incident.

fig.title: Offset mark, 29er
lines: Rounded with the kite going up
Crew, 30 s later: "We clipped the mark"

q: After a collision in which you holed Red's bow you retire at once and motor in. Red still lodges a protest and the committee finds you broke rule 10. Can it penalise you further?
a: No — retirement was the applicable penalty for the breach, so no further penalty; only a rule 2 finding could add a non-excludable DSQ
o: Yes — a retired boat can still be disqualified, which is worse than RET
Yes — a 20 % Scoring Penalty is added to your RET score
Yes — the committee can order you to miss the next race
why: Rule 60.5(c): a boat that has taken the applicable penalty shall not be penalised further unless the penalty for the rule broken is a non-excludable DSQ.

q: At the leeward mark you touched the buoy but took no turn, sure that Yellow had pushed you onto it. In the hearing the committee finds that Yellow kept clear and that you simply cut the corner. What is the outcome?
a: Disqualification — you were not compelled to break rule 31, so no exoneration, and you took no penalty
o: A One-Turn Penalty, which the committee converts into one place
No penalty — you genuinely believed you were exonerated
A 20 % Scoring Penalty for the mark contact
why: Rule 43.1(a) exonerates only a boat compelled by another's breach; rule 60.5(c): DSQ when a boat broke a rule and took no applicable penalty.

fig.title: Hearing: leeward mark
lines: You touched the buoy, no turn
Your claim: Yellow pushed you on
Facts: Yellow kept clear, you cut the corner

q: Passing the end of a long pier on the same tack, you are the inside boat and Blue, outside and to windward, is giving you room. You luff to clear the pier head and Blue has to respond sharply; she protests you under rule 16.1. Are you liable?
a: No — you were sailing within the room you were entitled to, so you are exonerated for breaking rule 16 against the boat obliged to give it
o: Yes — rule 16.1 applies to every course change, and you must take two turns
Yes — the inside boat at an obstruction has no right to alter course
No — rule 16 never applies at an obstruction
why: Rule 43.1(b): a boat sailing within the room she is entitled to is exonerated for breaking a rule of Section A, rule 15, 16 or 31 in that incident.

fig.note: You luff to clear the pier head; Blue must respond

q: Leeward mark, you are the inside windward boat with mark-room. Grey, outside and to leeward with right of way, gives you so little room that your hulls touch as you round — no damage. Grey protests you under rules 11 and 14. Result?
a: You are exonerated for both — you were sailing within your mark-room, and the contact caused no damage or injury; Grey should take a Two-Turns Penalty
o: You are penalised under rule 11 — the windward boat must keep clear whatever her mark-room
Both boats are penalised — any contact breaks rule 14 for both
You are penalised under rule 14 only, Grey under rule 18
why: Rule 43.1(b) exonerates a boat sailing within her mark-room for a Section A rule; rule 43.1(c) for rule 14 when there is no damage or injury.

fig.note: Grey gives too little room; hulls touch, no damage

q: Thirty seconds before the start, parked below the committee boat, you back your jib to drop astern and your transom bumps the boat behind, which is holding station normally. No damage. What do you owe?
a: A Two-Turns Penalty — a boat moving astern by backing a sail keeps clear of one that is not, and that is a Part 2 rule
o: Nothing — before the starting signal the rules of Part 2 do not apply
A One-Turn Penalty — pre-start contact is treated like touching a mark
Nothing — the boat behind was clear astern and had to keep clear of you
why: Rule 21.3 (Part 2 Section D): a boat moving astern by backing a sail keeps clear; rule 44.1 gives the Two-Turns Penalty.

fig.note: 0:30; you back the jib and drop onto Red

q: The sailing instructions say: "The Scoring Penalty, rule 44.3, applies; the penalty is two places." You take it and finish 4th in a 30-boat fleet. What is your score, and what happens to the boats behind you?
a: 6 points — and the boats behind you keep their scores, so the 5th and 6th boats stay on 5 and 6
o: 4 plus 20 % of 31, about 10 points — the places clause does not change the arithmetic
6 points, and the 5th and 6th boats move up to 4th and 5th
4 points — a places penalty is applied only to the series total
why: Rule 44.3(c): the score is worsened by the number of places stated in the NoR or SI, and the scores of other boats are not changed.

q: Milling about before the preparatory signal of a J/24 race, you are on port and force a starboard boat to tack away to avoid you. No contact. She hails "Protest". Can you be penalised?
a: No — you are not yet racing, and a boat not racing is not penalised for a Part 2 breach except rule 14 with injury or serious damage, or rule 23.1
o: Yes — Part 2 applies from the moment you are in the racing area, so take two turns
Yes — but only with a 20 % Scoring Penalty, not disqualification
No — rule 10 does not apply at all before the starting signal
why: Preamble to Part 2: a boat not racing shall not be penalised for breaking a Part 2 rule, except rule 14 with injury or serious damage, or rule 23.1.
ref: RRS Part 2 preamble, RRS definition Racing

A starboard boat tacks away to avoid you

q: After causing serious damage at the windward mark you decide to retire, as rule 44.1(b) requires. What do you do next?
a: Leave the course without interfering with boats still racing, and inform the race committee as the sailing instructions require
o: Sail the rest of the course anyway so that you are scored DNF rather than RET
Display a yellow flag and finish, so that the committee can score the penalty
Take two turns first and then retire, to cover both possibilities
why: Rule 23.1: a boat not racing shall not interfere with boats racing; the SI normally require a retiring boat to notify the race committee.

q: You are close-hauled on starboard, holding a steady course, when Blue on port hits your bow and hails "Protest — you bore away into me!" You did not change course. What do you do?
a: Keep racing without taking a penalty — you broke no rule; Blue should be taking two turns, and the hearing will decide the facts
o: Take a Two-Turns Penalty — in a collision both boats always take turns
Take a One-Turn Penalty as a goodwill gesture
Retire — a boat hit on a beat must assume she is at fault
why: Rule 10: Blue keeps clear; rule 44.1 only concerns a boat that may have broken a rule; the protest committee establishes the facts.

fig.note: Blue hits your bow and hails "Protest"

q: River course with a strong ebb. Rounding the windward mark in almost no wind, the current sets you sideways onto the buoy despite everything you try. Nobody else is near. Do you owe a penalty?
a: Yes — rule 31 does not ask whose fault it was; you touched the mark while racing, so take a One-Turn Penalty
o: No — a boat that touches a mark because of current or lack of wind is exonerated
No — exoneration applies whenever the contact was unavoidable
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, since there was no other boat to blame
why: Rule 31 is broken by the touch itself; exoneration under rule 43.1 needs another boat's breach or room entitlement.

fig.note: Ebb sets you sideways onto the buoy; no wind

q: Black flag preparatory signal, the race starts normally. You know you were in the triangle in the last minute, so you sail back round the pin end, restart behind the fleet and finish 2nd. How are you scored?
a: BFD — disqualified without a hearing; returning and restarting does not remove a black-flag penalty
o: 2nd — you corrected your error before starting, as under flag I
2nd with a 20 % Scoring Penalty added
OCS — a boat that restarts late is scored as not having started
why: Rule 30.4: a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing; only a postponement or abandonment before the start lifts it.

fig.title: Black flag, clean start
lines: You go back round the pin and restart

q: Flag U is displayed. In the last minute you realise part of your hull is inside the triangle, so you dip back round the pin end as you would under flag I and start cleanly after the signal. Does that save you?
a: No — flag U disqualifies her without a hearing; rounding an end is for flag I
o: Yes — sailing round an end of the line cures any starting error
Yes — flags I and U have the same round-an-end remedy
No — but the penalty is only 20 %, as under flag Z
why: Rule 30.3: UFD without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed; the round-an-end remedy belongs to rule 30.1.

fig.note: Flag U; you go back round the pin end

q: The results show ZFP against your name after a Z-flag start. You go to the race office to demand a hearing because you were "only just" inside the triangle. What will you be told?
a: That a Z-flag penalty is applied without a hearing — your only route is a request for redress if you think the committee made an error
o: That a hearing will be scheduled, as for any penalty
That the penalty will be reduced to 10 % because you were only just inside
That you can replace it with two turns before the next race
why: Rule 30.2: the 20 % penalty is applied without a hearing; a boat disputing the facts may request redress.

q: Arbitration under Appendix T. After hearing both of you, the arbitrator says the protest committee would probably find that you broke rule 11. What can you do now?
a: Accept a 30 % Post-Race Penalty, or let the protest go to a full hearing where you risk disqualification
o: Nothing — the arbitrator's opinion is the final decision
Take two turns ashore in front of the arbitrator
Accept a 20 % Scoring Penalty, as on the water
why: Appendix T4: after the arbitrator's opinion a boat may take the Post-Race Penalty (30 %) or the protest may proceed to a hearing.

q: Appendix T applies. In the incident you are protested for, the other boat's rudder was broken off and she withdrew from the regatta. You ask for an arbitration meeting to take the 30 % penalty. Will you get it?
a: No — when the arbitrator decides rule 44.1(b) may apply there is no arbitration and no Post-Race Penalty; it goes to a full hearing
o: Yes — any Part 2 incident can be settled by a 30 % Post-Race Penalty
Yes — but the penalty is raised to 50 % because of the damage
No — arbitration is only for incidents without a protest
why: Appendix T1(a) and T2: the Post-Race Penalty and the arbitration meeting are not available when rule 44.1(b) — injury or serious damage — may apply.
